summary: First English narrative for the Mawson-Mertz route choice of December 14, 1912, written from the case's structured facts.

narrative.hook: The crevasse took your companion, your tent, your best dogs and nearly all your food, and it did it in the time it takes to look up. You are five hundred kilometres from base with ten days of rations. Before dark you have to pick which way you walk home.
narrative.short_setup: December 14, 1912, on the plateau of King George V Land. Douglas Mawson's Far Eastern sledging party is three men: Mawson, the Swiss ski expert Xavier Mertz, and Lieutenant Belgrave Ninnis. Ninnis's sledge crosses a snow bridge that the other two have already crossed, and the bridge gives way. Gone with him: six of the best dogs, the tent, a spade, an ice-axe, and the great majority of the remaining food. What Mawson and Mertz have between them is roughly a week and a half of rations for two men, six weaker dogs with nothing at all to feed them, and a spare tent cover with no poles. Base is about five hundred kilometres away. There are two ways back, and the choice has to be made now.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The coast route bought something the plateau could not: more food, and other people. Down at the frozen sea there were seals, and a party carrying ten days of rations across five hundred kilometres needs a second source or it is simply running a clock. There was also a chance — thin, but not imaginary — of being sighted by the relief ship or by another sledging party working the coastline, which would convert the whole problem from 'can two exhausted men cover this distance' into 'can two exhausted men be found'. Those are very different problems, and only one of them has a solution that does not depend entirely on their own legs.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: The plateau was shorter, led to a fixed and known destination, and required no descent. That last part mattered more than usual, because the descent on offer ran through a glacier Mawson already knew to be heavily crevassed — worse ground than what had just killed Ninnis. And the sea ice at the bottom of it was not a guaranteed surface: this was close to midsummer, when breakup was likelier. The plateau had crevasses too, but the party had crossed some of this ground on the way out, which is not the same as safe but is not nothing either. Against a coastal gamble with two independent unknowns stacked in sequence, the direct line to a place they could find was the more conservative read.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: They took the plateau, the same day. Mawson recorded the reasoning: a descent to the frozen sea would be dangerous given how heavily crevassed the glacier there was, and he judged that with reasonable weather he and Mertz might make Winter Quarters on a week and a half of rations plus the six dogs, eaten progressively along the way. That is his own account, written afterward — his stated reasoning rather than an independent verification of it.
narrative.outcome_story: They walked, and they ate the dogs. From around January 1, Mertz declined sharply — fits, delirium — and he died on January 8, roughly a hundred miles short of base. Mawson went on alone. He cut his sledge down and stripped his load to essentials. On January 17 he went partway into a crevasse and survived only because his harness caught on the lip; he hauled himself out and afterward built a rope ladder so that a next time would not be the last time. He reached Aladdin's Cave near base and a blizzard pinned him there for a week. He walked into Winter Quarters on February 8, 1913 — a few hours after the relief ship Aurora had sailed. He and six men of a search party who had stayed behind spent an unplanned second Antarctic winter at Cape Denison before the ship came back in December 1913.
narrative.hindsight_analysis: This decision rates strongly, and it is worth being careful about why, because the obvious reason is the wrong one. The wrong reason is that Mawson survived. He survived by a harness catching on a lip of ice, which is not a property of the route. The right reason is visible at the moment of choosing. He had just been shown, in the most direct way available, what the ground could do — and the alternative required descending through terrain he independently knew to be worse, onto a surface whose stability at midsummer nobody could vouch for. That is two unknowns stacked in sequence, either of which ends everything, against a route with one known hazard and some prior familiarity. Declining to add the second gamble to an already desperate position is sound reasoning about risk, not merely a flinch after trauma. What has to be said alongside it is that the coast route's upside was real and was given up. Seals were genuine food and a sighting was a genuine alternative mechanism of rescue, and a food-desperate party could have defensibly gambled on them. The outcome, meanwhile, should not be allowed to settle anything in either direction. Mertz died, and the dog-meat diet that the plateau route required is one of two competing explanations for why — the 1969 hypervitaminosis-A hypothesis against a 2005 re-evaluation pointing to malnutrition, shock and an abrupt all-meat diet. The medical literature has not resolved it. And crucially, none of it could have counted against the decision in 1912: the toxic effects of eating sled-dog liver in these quantities were not established knowledge. You cannot mark down a choice for failing to account for something nobody yet knew. The deepest limit on judging this case is simpler still. The coast route was never taken. There is no counterfactual to compare against, only a road not walked, and the honest position is that the decision was well-made and the outcome was terrible, and that those two facts do not have to be reconciled.
narrative.decision_principle: When two dangers sit in sequence and either one alone can end you, their risks do not average — they compound. A path with one known hazard can beat a path with two unverified ones even when the second path has the better prize at the end.
narrative.longform_story:
The snow bridge held for two sledges and broke under the third.

That is most of what there is to say about how it happened. On December 14, 1912, on the high plateau of King George V Land, Douglas Mawson and Xavier Mertz crossed a covered crevasse without knowing it was there. Belgrave Ninnis, following with the rear sledge, did not. When Mertz looked back, there was a hole and no Ninnis.

What went into the crevasse with him is the part that turned an accident into a crisis. Six of the party's best dogs. The tent. A spade and an ice-axe. And the great majority of the food — because on a sledging party you distribute your load by likelihood of loss, and the rear sledge, following a track already tested twice, was reckoned the safest place for the supplies.

Mawson and Mertz called down into the crevasse for hours. Then they took stock. Between them they had roughly a week and a half of rations for two men. They had six surviving dogs, weaker than the ones lost, and not a scrap of food for them. They had a spare tent cover and no poles. Base — Winter Quarters, at Cape Denison — was about five hundred kilometres away.

And they had to choose a route before they did anything else, because the two options diverged immediately.

One ran down to the coast. Get to the frozen sea and there would be seals, which is to say food that was not the dogs, and a coastline where the relief ship or another of the expedition's sledging parties might conceivably be working. That second possibility is easy to undervalue at this distance. It changes the nature of the problem. Without it, two men have to cover five hundred kilometres on what they carry and what they can kill; with it, there is a chance they only have to get somewhere they can be seen.

The other retraced the plateau, roughly along the outward track, straight at a fixed destination, with nothing to eat but the dogs.

Mawson's own reasoning, as he set it down afterward: the descent to the frozen sea would be dangerous, because the glacier there was heavily crevassed. He judged that with reasonable weather he and Mertz could make Winter Quarters on the rations they had plus the six dogs eaten progressively along the way. They started back over the plateau the same day.

It is worth laying out what makes that a strong decision, because the easy answer is wrong.

The easy answer is that Mawson lived, so he chose correctly. He lived because on January 17 his sledge harness caught on the lip of a crevasse he had already fallen into. That is not a property of the route; it is a piece of luck about a buckle. Outcomes reached that way do not certify the reasoning that led to them.

The real case is one he could make on December 14. He had just been shown what this ground did to a man who trusted it. The alternative asked him to descend through terrain he independently knew to be worse — more heavily crevassed than the plateau that had just taken Ninnis — and then to travel on sea ice whose stability, this close to midsummer, nobody could vouch for. That is two independent unknowns arranged in sequence, either of which is fatal on its own. Risks like that do not average out. They stack. Against them stood a route with one known hazard type, on ground the party had at least partly seen, leading to a place they knew how to find.

Declining to add a second gamble to a position already this bad is not flinching. It is a correct reading of how sequential risks behave.

What should be said in the same breath is that the coast route's upside was not imaginary and was genuinely surrendered. Seal meat would have been real food. A sighting would have been a real rescue. A party with ten days of rations and five hundred kilometres to cover, doing the arithmetic honestly, might reasonably have decided that the arithmetic did not work and that a gamble was therefore the rational move. Both readings are defensible. The record supports the one Mawson took; it does not make the other foolish.

Then the journey.

The dogs went one at a time. Mertz began to fail around the first of January — fits, delirium, a collapse that was fast even by the standards of men who had been starving for weeks. He died on January 8, about a hundred miles from base. Mawson buried him, cut his sledge in half with a pocket tool, discarded everything that was not survival, and walked on alone.

On January 17 the ground opened again. He went in, and the harness held, and he hung over the dark on a rope he then had to climb. He got out. Then he built himself a rope ladder and fixed it to his harness, on the reasoning that there would be a next time and he might not be conscious for it.

He reached Aladdin's Cave, the supply cache near base, and a blizzard held him there for a week — seven days, within sight of the end. He walked into Winter Quarters on February 8, 1913. The Aurora had sailed a few hours earlier. Six men who had stayed behind to search for the Far Eastern Party were still there, and with Mawson they spent another full Antarctic winter at Cape Denison before the ship returned in December.

So what killed Mertz? The honest answer is that we do not know. In 1969 Cleland and Southcott proposed hypervitaminosis A, from the dogs' vitamin-A-rich livers, and for decades that was the standard account. In 2005 Denise Carrington-Smith argued in the Medical Journal of Australia that the quantity of liver eaten was too small for acute toxicity, and pointed instead to severe malnutrition, the psychological trauma of losing Ninnis and the dogs, and the physiological shock of an abrupt shift to an almost all-meat diet. The literature has not settled between them.

This matters for how the decision is scored, and it matters in a specific direction. The dog-meat diet was a consequence of the plateau route — it was the route's food plan. If the livers killed Mertz, the route contributed to his death. But the toxic effects of eating sled-dog liver in these quantities were not established medical knowledge in 1912. Nobody in Antarctica that summer could have factored it in, and a decision cannot be marked down for failing to account for something not yet known. Whatever the medical verdict eventually is, it belongs to the outcome column and not to the judgment column.

The last and largest limit on assessing any of this is the simplest. The coast route was never taken. There is no way to know whether it would have found seals or found open water, whether a ship would have passed or nothing would have. Two men chose a road and walked it, and the other road stayed hypothetical forever.

Which leaves the case where it should be left. The decision was well-made on the information available, on grounds that hold without knowing the ending. The outcome was terrible: one man dead, another nearly so, a ship missed by hours and a year of life spent waiting for the next one. Both things are true. They do not need to be reconciled, and a serious account of decision-making under uncertainty is precisely one that can hold them apart.
